clue.text: French novelist foreshadows Warwick Deeping character

definitions.meaning: Louis ... (1866-1941) was a French novelist of Algeria and the Mediterranean
... du Guesclin is the hero of Deeping's historical novel ... of Brittany

explanation.surface: A French writer is said to anticipate a figure from an English novelist's fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foreshadows' only joins the two definitions, as if the French writer came first in time.
explanation.definitionFit: The same name belongs both to a French writer of fiction and to the Breton knight who heads Deeping's 1908 romance.

clue.text: Pigeon I prepare for successors of Alexander

indicators.note: to prepare the words is to work them up afresh, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters for the anagram

explanation.surface: Someone readies a pigeon for the heirs of a Macedonian conqueror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepare' rearranges PIGEONI. The name, Greek for 'offspring', is applied to the sons of the generals who divided Alexander's empire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Epigoni were the next generation of rulers after the Diadochi, the generals who inherited Alexander the Great's empire.

clue.text: Unduly subjective subject of Meredith

parts.note: the self-absorbed Sir Willoughby Patterne is the title figure of George Meredith's 1879 novel

explanation.surface: A self-centred figure is the theme of a Victorian novelist's book.
explanation.walkthrough: The play on 'subjective' and 'subject' points to a person wrapped up in himself, and to the novel that takes him as its subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's novel is named for its self-absorbed hero, a man who sees everything only in terms of himself.

clue.text: "All things-eternally as they were in their proper places" (Traherne)

definitions.text: "All things-eternally as they were in their proper places" (Traherne)

parts.words: "All things-eternally as they were in their proper places" (Traherne)
parts.note: the missing verb completes a sentence from Thomas Traherne's Centuries of Meditations about things staying put for ever

explanation.surface: A line from the seventeenth-century mystic Thomas Traherne with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks the gap: the full line reads 'All things abided eternally as they were in their proper places'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing past-tense verb means remained or stayed, fitting things that kept to their places for ever.

clue.text: Where Priestley's oeuvre took a perilous turn

definitions.text: Where Priestley's oeuvre took a perilous turn

parts.words: Where Priestley's oeuvre took a perilous turn
parts.note: a risky bend in a road, and also the title of J. B. Priestley's 1932 play

explanation.surface: A critic remarks on the point at which a writer's career went off the rails.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like literary criticism, but 'perilous turn' is a literal description of the play's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Priestley's first play is named for a hazardous bend, a moment when a careless remark sends the story somewhere risky.

clue.text: His plays are set to some reportedly vile music

definitions.text: His plays are set to some reportedly vile music

parts.words: His plays are set to some reportedly vile music
parts.note: Kurt Weill, whose German name is said with a V sound, wrote the music for this dramatist's Threepenny Opera

explanation.surface: A complaint that a playwright's works have been set to dreadful tunes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vile' is not a judgement: in German, Weill is pronounced as 'vile', so the music is by Kurt Weill, the dramatist's collaborator.
explanation.definitionFit: The German dramatist's best-known stage works, like The Threepenny Opera, carry scores by his partner Kurt Weill.

clue.text: Author of Greenmantle an English Victorian poet?

parts.note: John Buchan wrote the 1916 spy thriller Greenmantle
taken as written

explanation.surface: Was the writer of a wartime thriller also a Victorian poet?
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Buchanan was born in England, though he is often called Scottish, so the definition ends with a question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Buchanan was a Victorian poet and critic, remembered for attacking the 'Fleshly School' of the Pre-Raphaelites.

clue.text: Asch, in a way, that is right teller

indicators.note: to arrange the name in a way is to put its letters in some other order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The writer Sholem Asch, in a manner of speaking, is the right person to narrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' is the anagram signal. 'teller' looks like a storyteller, which suits the Yiddish novelist Sholem Asch, but it means the bank clerk.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank teller is the clerk who pays out and takes in money at the counter.

clue.text: Part of verb goes on ahead, say, indicating strain

indicators.note: one piece goes on before the other, so the grammar word is followed by the headland

parts.note: a tense is a grammatical form of a verb, such as past or future
a ness is a headland, read here as 'a head' in the geographical sense

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson about verbs and moving forward, ending in nervous tension.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ahead' splits as 'a head', and a ness is a head of land jutting into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Strain and the state of being taut or anxious are the same nervous condition.

clue.text: Classic satires, so to speak

parts.note: the drunken woodland companions of Dionysus in Greek myth, whose kind sounds like 'satires'

explanation.surface: A remark about classical works of mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so to speak' hints at sound: these figures are satyrs, which is said like 'satires', and 'Classic' means classical mythology.
explanation.definitionFit: The followers of Dionysus led by Silenus are satyr-like woodland figures, plural of Silenus.

clue.text: His major work concerned some people

definitions.text: His major work concerned some people

parts.words: His major work concerned some people
parts.note: Harold ... best-known book is the 1927 sketch collection called Some People

explanation.surface: A writer's main book was about a handful of individuals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some people' reads as a vague phrase but is the exact title of the book.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Nicolson, diplomat and diarist, is best remembered for his witty portrait collection Some People.

clue.text: Hero begs abjectly in Roman palace

indicators.note: acting abjectly, the words are thrown into a wretched state and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, eight letters for the anagram

explanation.surface: A fallen hero pleads miserably inside an Italian residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abjectly' rearranges HEROBEGS; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Palazzo Borghese in Rome was the seat of the noble Borghese family.

clue.text: Laertes did not go short of it

definitions.text: Laertes did not go short of it

parts.words: Laertes did not go short of it
parts.note: in Hamlet, Polonius gives his son a long string of maxims before he sails for France

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean young man was never lacking something.
explanation.walkthrough: Polonius's farewell speech, with 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be', is a heap of counsel for Laertes.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius's farewell speech to his son is a set of precepts and counsel on how to behave.

clue.text: One of Larry Niven's extremes?

parts.note: Larry Niven published a story collection titled ..., so one of them is a single boundary

explanation.surface: A question about the outer edges of a science-fiction writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Niven's 1985 collection is called Limits; one of those is the singular.
explanation.definitionFit: An extreme is a boundary or furthest point, and Niven's book takes the plural of that word as its title.

clue.text: Voltairean epic with part for a maid

definitions.text: Voltairean epic with part for a maid

parts.words: Voltairean epic with part for a maid
parts.note: Voltaire's mock-epic on Joan of Arc, the Maid of Orleans, whose French title means 'the maid'

explanation.surface: A Voltaire poem includes a role for a servant girl.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'maid' sounds like a domestic part, but the title is French for 'the maid', Joan of Arc.
explanation.definitionFit: Voltaire's satirical poem about Joan of Arc takes the French word for virgin or maid as its title.

clue.text: You a merry sort of gypsy gentleman!

parts.words: You a merry sort of gypsy gentleman!
parts.note: George Borrow's 1857 novel is named for a gentleman who befriends Romani travellers

explanation.surface: An exclamation greeting a cheerful traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: The title of George Borrow's sequel to Lavengro means 'Romani gentleman'.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrow's title combines the Romani word for gentleman with the people's name, describing Borrow himself.

clue.text: When we had daily cleaning, according to Henry Reed

definitions.text: When we had daily cleaning, according to Henry Reed

parts.words: When we had daily cleaning, according to Henry Reed
parts.note: Henry Reed's war poem Naming of Parts opens: 'Today we have naming of parts. ... we had daily cleaning.'

explanation.surface: A soldier recalls the routine of daily cleaning in a famous poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening of Naming of Parts sets 'Today' against the day before, when the recruits cleaned their rifles.
explanation.definitionFit: The day before today is when Reed's recruits had their cleaning drill, in the poem's opening lines.

clue.text: Like Goldsmith's version of Hamlet?

parts.note: a hamlet is a small village, and Oliver Goldsmith's poem is The ... Village

explanation.surface: A query about Oliver Goldsmith's take on Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet' looks like Shakespeare's play; it is a small village, as in Goldsmith's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldsmith's poem laments a village left empty when its people were driven away.

clue.text: Denigrate the doctrine of Roman religion

parts.note: to pan a play is to criticise it harshly
taken as written
an ism is any distinctive doctrine or theory

explanation.surface: Someone attacks the teachings of ancient Rome's faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link word. The definition is loose: Roman religion had many gods, the Pantheon being their temple.
explanation.definitionFit: The belief that God is in everything, or the worship of all gods together, as at Rome's Pantheon.

clue.text: Bathing beauties tangled in reeds

indicators.note: tangled suggests the letters are knotted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters for the anagram

explanation.surface: Swimmers caught up among waterside plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in reeds' looks like where the beauties are trapped, but those letters are the anagram fodder for 'tangled'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea nymphs in Greek myth, daughters of Nereus, were lovely creatures who lived in the water.

clue.text: Cricket trophy recalled by Grazia Deledda

definitions.meaning: the urn contested in Test matches between England and Australia
Cenere, a 1904 novel by the Sardinian Nobel laureate Grazia Deledda, means the burnt remains of a fire

explanation.surface: A sporting prize brought to mind by an Italian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the England–Australia cricket series and its tiny urn trophy; Deledda's novel Cenere has the same title in English.
explanation.definitionFit: The burnt remains of the bails gave the cricket urn its name, and Deledda's novel title translates as the same residue.

clue.text: Spirit of French work in progress?

definitions.meaning: zest or high spirits, a word borrowed from French
the French phrase '...' means under way, for a job being done

explanation.surface: A French phrase about the spirit of an unfinished work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' joins the two definitions. 'Work in progress' sounds like a manuscript, but it means simply 'in progress'.
explanation.definitionFit: Liveliness or enthusiasm is the English sense; the French phrase means under way or in progress.

clue.text: Average part for Madame Arcati

definitions.meaning: middling, in between large and small
Madame Arcati is the eccentric spiritualist in Noel Coward's comedy Blithe Spirit

explanation.surface: An ordinary role for a character in a Noel Coward play.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Arcati holds a séance in Blithe Spirit, so her role is a spiritualist.
explanation.definitionFit: Middling in size describes the first sense; a spiritualist who contacts the dead is the second.

clue.text: "--s, long dust, will come and go" (R. Brooke)

definitions.text: "--s, long dust, will come and go" (R. Brooke)

parts.words: "--s, long dust, will come and go" (R. Brooke)
parts.note: a line from Rupert Brooke's Grantchester about the clergymen of the village

explanation.surface: A gap in a line of Rupert Brooke's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line in Grantchester: 'Curates, long dust, will come and go / On lissom, clerical, printless toe'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names an assistant clergyman, who in Brooke's poem treads lightly across the meadows.

clue.text: Small work in Italian (or possibly German?)

definitions.text: Small work in Italian (or possibly German?)

parts.words: Small work in Italian (or possibly German?)
parts.note: an Italian diminutive meaning 'little opera', a genre associated with Vienna and German composers

explanation.surface: A note on a short piece in Italian, or perhaps in German.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is Italian for 'little work', but the light opera form is closely linked with Vienna and Johann Strauss.
explanation.definitionFit: A light, short musical stage play; the Italian diminutive of 'opera', itself Latin for work.

clue.text: Visualizer of Romola

parts.note: Frederic ... drew the illustrations for George Eliot's novel Romola in the Cornhill Magazine

explanation.surface: Who first pictured a George Eliot heroine?
explanation.walkthrough: Romola was serialised in 1862-63 with engravings by the painter Frederic Leighton.
explanation.definitionFit: Leighton, later President of the Royal Academy, gave Eliot's Florentine novel its pictures.

clue.text: Unseasonal summer recorded by Howells

parts.note: William Dean Howells wrote the 1886 novel ... Summer, named for a warm autumn spell

explanation.surface: An American novelist chronicles warm weather out of season.
explanation.walkthrough: A warm spell in autumn is called an Indian summer; Howells used the phrase as a title.
explanation.definitionFit: The first word of the phrase for a late, out-of-season warm spell, and of Howells's novel title.

clue.text: What Twenty Years After inevitably did

definitions.text: What Twenty Years After inevitably did

parts.words: What Twenty Years After inevitably did
parts.note: Dumas's Twenty Years After is the sequel to The Three Musketeers, so it came next

explanation.surface: A remark on what happened two decades later.
explanation.walkthrough: Twenty Years After looks like a time span, but it is Dumas's sequel, which followed The Three Musketeers.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow as a consequence or in sequence; a sequel does this to its predecessor.

clue.text: A degree in Aryan version of Sanskrit epic poem

indicators.note: the article and the degree are placed in the middle of the rearranged word
a version of the word gives its letters in another order

parts.note: MA, Master of Arts, is a university degree

explanation.surface: A degree in an Aryan reworking of an ancient Indian poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of' is the anagram signal and makes RAYAN; the inserted letters go in just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ramayana tells the story of Rama and is one of the two great Sanskrit epics of India.
